source.title: A Year of Bread
source.text:
A Year of Bread

I did not set out to become a person who bakes bread. It happened the way most of my habits happen: sideways, by accident, while I was trying to do something else. In the spring I had promised myself I would learn to cook three proper meals, and somewhere between a failed soup and a passable curry I watched a short video of a baker in San Francisco folding wet dough over itself with one hand. The dough looked alive. It stretched and resisted and relaxed, and the baker — a calm man named Chad Robertson, whose bakery, Tartine, I would later read everything about — said something that stuck with me: bread is not made, it is raised. I closed the video, opened a shopping list, and wrote down flour.

The first loaf was a disaster, and I want to be precise about the kind of disaster it was. It was not burned. It was not raw. It was dense in a way that seemed to violate physics, as if I had baked a paperweight that smelled like beer. I had followed a recipe from a website, measured everything in cups because I did not yet own a scale, and kneaded the dough with the grim determination of a man wringing out a towel. My wife tapped the crust with a spoon, listened to the dull thunk, and said, kindly, that we could still use it for sandwiches if we sliced it very thin. We could not use it for sandwiches.

What went wrong, I learned over the following weeks, was almost everything, but the biggest problem was invisible. Bread rises because yeast — a living organism — eats the sugars in flour and breathes out carbon dioxide, and the gluten in the dough traps those small breaths like a net catching fish. My dough had almost no gluten development and my yeast was half dead, so there was nothing to catch and nothing to breathe. The recipe had told me what to do but not what to notice. That distinction became the theme of my entire year: the difference between following instructions and paying attention.

So I bought a scale. This sounds like a small thing, and it cost less than a pizza, but it changed everything, because baking is chemistry wearing an apron. A cup of flour can weigh anywhere from 120 to 160 grams depending on how you scoop it, which means my careful cup measurements had been introducing errors of up to thirty percent. With a scale, the same recipe produced the same dough twice in a row for the first time. Repetition made comparison possible, and comparison made learning possible. I started keeping a notebook: date, flour, water, salt, time, temperature, and a one-line verdict. The first verdict reads, in full, "better brick."

The notebook taught me my second lesson, which is that water is a character in this story, not a background prop. Bakers talk about hydration — the weight of water as a percentage of the weight of flour — the way sailors talk about wind. A stiff sixty-percent dough is easy to shape and forgiving to handle, and it bakes into a tight, even crumb. An eighty-percent dough sticks to your hands, your counter, your soul, and slumps like a jellyfish when you try to shape it — but if you can manage it, it bakes into an open, glossy crumb with holes you could put a thumb through. For a month I stayed at sixty-five percent, and every week I added a little more water, the way you wade into a cold lake.

Then came the starter. Commercial yeast is a single domesticated species sold in packets, reliable as a light switch. A sourdough starter is a small unruly civilization: wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria living together in a jar of flour and water, eating and multiplying and producing the acids that give sourdough its name and its flavor. You do not buy a starter; you raise one. For ten days I fed a jar of flour paste every morning like a tamagotchi, and for ten days it did nothing except smell faintly of socks. On the eleventh day it doubled in size overnight and smelled like green apples and vinegar, and I felt a pride so far out of proportion to the achievement that I photographed the jar and sent the picture to three people, none of whom replied.

Baking with the starter meant surrendering my schedule. Commercial yeast works in hours; a starter works in its own time, which depends on temperature, on the flour, on how recently it was fed, on factors I still do not fully understand. A dough mixed at eight in the morning might be ready to shape at two in the afternoon in July and at six in the evening in November. The bakers I read all said the same thing in different words: watch the dough, not the clock. The dough tells you when it is ready — it grows by half, it turns smooth and slightly domed, it jiggles when you shake the bowl, and small bubbles appear at the edges like the first stars coming out.

I ruined many loaves learning to read those signs. Under-fermented dough bakes into a pale, tight loaf with a raw taste, because the yeast never finished its work. Over-fermented dough is worse: the gluten net, digested by too many hours of acid and enzymes, collapses like wet paper, and the loaf spreads into a sad pancake the moment it hits the oven. The window between the two is wide enough once you know it, and invisible until you do. My notebook from that stretch of summer is a museum of flat bread, and each entry ends with a shorter and angrier verdict, until one page in August just says "why."

The answer to "why," it turned out, was heat — the last major character in the story. A professional bread oven does two things a home oven does not: it holds ferocious, even heat, and it fills itself with steam at the start of the bake. Steam matters because it keeps the surface of the loaf soft for the first ten minutes, letting the bread expand to its full size before the crust sets. Without steam, the crust hardens early, like a plaster cast, and the loaf stays small no matter how lively the dough was. The home baker's trick is to bake inside a heavy covered cast-iron pot, which traps the loaf's own moisture as steam. The day I first used one, the loaf leapt so high above the rim that the seam I had scored burst open like a grin, and I stood in front of the oven window and laughed.

That loaf — notebook entry forty-one — was the first one I would have paid money for. The crust crackled when it cooled, ticking like a car engine shutting off, a sound bakers call singing. The crumb was open and glossy, the flavor deep and faintly sour, with a sweetness in the middle I had not expected. We ate half of it standing at the counter with nothing but butter, and I remember thinking that the distance between this loaf and the first brick was nine months, forty failures, and perhaps four genuinely important lessons, none of which had appeared anywhere in that first recipe.

I want to be honest about the costs, because the internet version of this hobby is all golden crusts and no arithmetic. I burned a bag of flour a week for a year, which is not expensive as hobbies go, but is not free. I gave hours to it — folding dough at odd moments, waking early to preheat the oven, staying home on afternoons when the dough was almost ready. There were weeks when the baking felt less like a craft and more like a second job with a demanding, silent boss who lived in a jar. Anyone who tells you a sourdough habit fits neatly into a busy life is either better organized than I am or lying.

And yet the habit held, through the failures and the flat months, for a reason I only understood later, and which has very little to do with bread itself. Everything else I make for a living is made of words and pixels and can be revised forever; nothing is ever finished, only abandoned. A loaf of bread is finished. It comes out of the oven at four o'clock and it is exactly what it is: you cannot patch it, update it, or roll it back. At first that finality terrified me, and then it became the entire point.
